name: Sgt. Carl Mayhew
origin: Woodside, Queens; son of a transit motorman
occupation: NYPD sergeant on administrative duty at Midtown Central; Teddy's former partner; testified in 1972 and kept his badge
want: Stay useful enough to powerful men to survive until his pension in 1976.
need: Say out loud what he did in 1971.
secret: He testified against six men and left out the two who mattered, Lisle and Wurtz. Lisle steered the prosecutors in return. He's been owned ever since.

speech.pattern: Brotherly and sentimental; says 'we' for things he did; calls Teddy 'kid'; quotes invented old songs; sweats through his jokes.
samples: Kid, the pad never died. It just went to law school.
I gave them six guys so you'd never have to give them one. You're welcome.
Walk with me. Like old times. Broadway, nice and slow, uptown.

haunts.why: Desk at the back; everyone stops talking when he walks by
Drinks alone at the end of the rail
Asks Teddy to meet him where he used to stand his post

arc.act1: Makes the offer on Broadway and recruits Teddy as a civilian collector.
arc.act2: Runs Teddy and starts to fear him. Learns about the wire or the copy (end of Act 2).
arc.act3: The resignation night panics him. In M25 he tells Teddy the truth in the same car, then either flips or runs.

visual.silhouette: Heavy, ruddy, hat pushed back; sport coat carried over the arm in the heat.
visual.wardrobe: Short-sleeve dress shirts with sweat rings, a clip-on tie, a plaid sport coat, brown crepe-soled shoes.
props: racing form folded to the late double
a station-house key he isn't supposed to have

name: Howard Lisle
origin: Rochester, New York; Columbia Law; assistant DA 1951–73
occupation: Attorney: 'real estate and trade association counsel'; architect of the new pad
want: Build a system that runs without envelopes, and be appointed to a city board by Christmas.
need: None he'd accept. The game shows what his tidiness costs.
secret: As an assistant DA he sold the outcomes of cases. The 1971 meet in Mayhew's car was one of those sales. Teddy is the only living witness who wasn't paid.

speech.pattern: Soft, precise and unhurried; legal phrasing followed by a plain kicker; never says 'money', always 'consideration' or 'fees'.
samples: Envelopes are evidence, Sergeant. Invoices are overhead.
Nobody is being evicted. They're being relocated, with a bonus. Read it.
I don't break laws. I read them more carefully than the men who wrote them.

haunts.why: Eleventh floor; he can see the Corwin's roof tank from his window
12:40 every weekday, same stool, same tuna on rye: a tail-able routine
Afternoon meetings in the lobby, never upstairs

edges.note: Has never once asked about her pension.

arc.act1: Buys the Corwin through Nick's name. Teddy photographs him at lunch (M5).
arc.act2: Turns the surcharge, the tax and the relocations into one ledger. Recruits Augie's successor.
arc.act3: Moves to close the syndicate before Labor Day: plea deals, the arson plan, a bid for Mayhew's silence. His fate follows Branch B.

visual.silhouette: Tall, thin and narrow-shouldered; walks with his hands behind his back; never hurries.
visual.wardrobe: Dove-grey tropical-weight suits, starched white shirts, regimental tie, horn-rimmed glasses, polished black wingtips.
props: the morning paper folded to the bond tables

name: Lt. Dennis Wurtz
origin: Bay Ridge, Brooklyn; Navy in the Pacific; NYPD since 1948
occupation: Lieutenant commanding the plainclothes 'conditions' team at Midtown Central (invented unit)
want: Retire in 1976 on thirty years with a boat in Florida, paid for twice.
need: None. He's the weather the others have to survive.
secret: He keeps duplicate photographs and arrest reports in a rented coin locker in Penn Station. It's his insurance against Lisle, and the game's most valuable object after the ledger.

speech.pattern: A jovial bully. Talks about his diet and his boat, threatens through compliments and uses sports metaphors.
samples: Lovely evening. Shame if the precinct had to notice how lovely.
Fifty a week is a tax. Seventy-five is a tax with a smile. Smile.
Knapp was weather. Weather passes. I'm climate.

haunts.why: Back door, after dark
Sweeps that end in envelopes
Informants under the trees
Locker 4-something; he checks it every Friday

edges.note: Distrusts the man and loves the system.
Suspects a leak; hasn't found it.

arc.act1: Raises the tax on the strip.
arc.act2: Squeezes the club and the showroom, and protects the brownout job for a cut.
arc.act3: Cleans house after the resignation: burns informants and hunts the photo file. His locker is the endgame lever (M27).

visual.silhouette: Big and thick-necked with a crew cut; leans on things; takes up doorways.
visual.wardrobe: Short-sleeve knit polo, maroon windbreaker, grey slacks, white sneakers (the plainclothes giveaway), a thin gold chain.
props: keys to an unmarked green sedan

name: Ruth Calloway
origin: Bedford-Stuyvesant, Brooklyn; Brooklyn Law (nights); worked in Lisle's DA bureau 1965–72
occupation: Investigator with the Special Prosecutor's office (a real institution, though she is invented and holds no real post)
want: One case that sticks above the rank of sergeant.
need: Admit that her witnesses are people she's using.
secret: Her funding line runs out in September. The 'protection' she offers Teddy lasts weeks, not years, and she hasn't told him.

speech.pattern: Crisp and deadpan; asks questions she already knows the answers to; Brooklyn shows under the law-school polish when she's tired.
samples: I'm not asking you to be brave, Mr. Arce. I'm asking you to be audible.
Everybody in your building is a witness. Most just don't know it yet.
I have a budget for coffee and a budget for you. Guess which is bigger.

haunts.why: Lunch-counter meets; crowds hide conversations
Parked surveillance across from Lisle's office
Reads property records in the reading room

arc.act2: Approaches Teddy (M12, Branch A). Either runs him on a wire or loses him.
arc.act3: Offers Nick a deal. Her deadline makes her reckless. Her ending depends on who gets the ledger.

visual.silhouette: Medium height, quick walk, arms full of files; glasses pushed up into her hair.
visual.wardrobe: Belted shirtwaist dresses or a dark pantsuit, flat shoes, a tan raincoat in any weather.

name: August “Augie” Lomax
origin: Hell's Kitchen; drove trucks from 1934; union man who fought the old trucking rackets
occupation: Dispatcher-boss of the Seventh Avenue Carriers' Association (invented trucking combine)
want: Keep 'his' streets for his drivers after he's gone.
need: See that the surcharge made him the thing he spent the 1940s fighting.
secret: He's sick, and he's quietly selling the Association to Lisle's people. His drivers think he's immortal.

speech.pattern: Barked numbers and street names; drivers' slang; sentimental about trucks and suspicious of people.
samples: Thirty-Seventh's a parking lot seven to ten. That's not traffic. That's my office.
Pay less and see who shows up on your block with a truck.
I drove these streets when your father was in short pants. Don't tell me routes.

haunts.why: Glass dispatch booth over the bays
Watches the morning jam like a general
Afternoon beer with drivers

arc.act1: The surcharge is everywhere, and Augie's name is on it.
arc.act2: Brownout logistics. Protects his drivers and sells them out at the same time.
arc.act3: Squeezed to flip. Hector betrays him first. A last morning in the booth.

visual.silhouette: Squat, bald under a flat cap, rolling walk; jaw always working a cigar.
visual.wardrobe: Green work shirt with a name patch, suspenders, grey work trousers, steel-toe boots.

name: Carmen Arce
origin: Mayagüez, Puerto Rico; came in 1948; ILGWU member since 1949
occupation: Sewing-machine operator at Feld Frocks, W 37th St; Penn South co-op resident
want: Three more years at the machine, her pension, and her son at her table on Sundays.
need: Say out loud that she knew about the envelopes.
secret: Feld is moving the shop to Ponce. She found out in June and hasn't told Teddy, because he'll try to fix it.

speech.pattern: Spanish and English mid-sentence; union vocabulary; scolds with love; proverbs; gives orders as questions.
samples: Mijo, you look like a man who hasn't eaten since the Korean War.
Forty years at a machine. Now they want me to train my replacement in Ponce.
The union built this building. Nobody sells it while I live in it.

haunts.why: Her machine, third row, by the window
Bodega and botanica
Benches between the towers; the co-op meeting room

edges.note: Thirty years; he told her first.

arc.act1: Sunday dinner. Sees through Teddy at once.
arc.act2: The shop's move to Ponce comes out. She joins Mei-Lin's severance fight.
arc.act3: Brings the garment operators to the march, and tells Teddy what she knew.

visual.silhouette: Small and quick, forward-leaning; glasses on a chain.
visual.wardrobe: Print shirtwaist dress, a cardigan in any weather, union pin, sensible black shoes.

name: Odessa Pruitt
origin: Savannah, Georgia; came to New York in 1929
occupation: Retired hotel laundress (thirty years in a big hotel's laundry); Corwin resident in room 1104 since 1956; head of the tenants' committee
want: Keep her room and the window that faces the Empire State.
need: Let younger people lead, and let herself be helped.
secret: She's two months behind on rent because she's been paying for Mr. Hollis's heart medicine. A court notice is hidden in her Bible.

speech.pattern: Church cadence; formal address ('Mr. Arce'); exact dates; scripture paraphrased into threats.
samples: Mr. Arce, I've lived in eleven-oh-four since 1956. I intend to die in it. Not soon.
Lawyers write long because they're scared of short words. Like 'no.'
Bring the chairs down to the lobby. If they want us out, they can carry us.

haunts.why: Her lobby chair, facing the desk
Newsstand and pharmacy
Sunday afternoons by the fountain

edges.note: Disapproves of the buyout; understands it.
Wants to see the owner's face.

arc.act1: Rallies the lobby against the vacate notices.
arc.act3: Leads the march (M28). Meets Nick face to face (M30).

visual.silhouette: Tall and slight, walks with a cane, never stoops.
visual.wardrobe: Print dresses, a church hat for any official business, white cotton gloves, a cameo brooch.

name: Ray Bauer
origin: Newark, New Jersey; pinball-route operator in the 1950s
occupation: Operates three peep and game arcades on 42nd St and Eighth Ave and the bar concession at two Eighth Ave hotels
want: Sell to Lisle's conversion scheme at a good price and become respectable.
secret: He's been Calloway's informant since 1973. Wurtz knows there's a leak and is getting closer.

speech.pattern: Salesman patter; malapropisms; nervous laugh; never finishes a threat.
samples: I sell quarters, Teddy. What people watch for a quarter is between them and God.
I pay Wurtz, I pay the landlord, I pay the fire inspector. Who pays me?
Legit. That's the word. I'm gonna be so legit you'll be bored.

haunts.why: Office above the change booth
Checks the bar's register; Rita watches him do it
2 a.m. eggs

arc.act1: A comic, venal fixture on the Deuce.
arc.act2: Squeezed between Wurtz and Calloway, he sells Delphine's habits to one of them.
arc.act3: Exposed after the resignation night. Whether he lives depends on what the leads do in M27.

visual.silhouette: Thin and restless; greying pompadour; never fully still.
visual.wardrobe: Orange print shirts, a white belt, tinted glasses, two-tone loafers.
props: transistor radio tuned to the races

name: Eleni Varelas
origin: Kastoria, Greece; came in 1950 to marry Nick
occupation: Keeps the books at Varelas & Co.
want: Make Nick sell the hotels and save the firm.
need: Stop protecting Nick from her own numbers.
secret: She knows about the double pledge. She has opened a separate account under her maiden name and is ready to leave.

speech.pattern: Quiet and dry; switches between Greek and English; exact figures; calls him 'Nikos' when she's angry.
samples: Nikos, the vault holds four hundred coats. The bank thinks it holds nine hundred.
In this family I'm the one who reads. You're the one who signs.
Summer is when furriers go broke politely.

haunts.why: Glass office overlooking the cutting floor
Her own account, under her maiden name

arc.act2: Opposes the vault scheme, then makes it work properly because Nick would botch it.
arc.act3: Gives Nick an ultimatum. She stays or leaves depending on what he does with the Corwin.

visual.silhouette: Elegant and still; sits upright; reading glasses on a chain.
visual.wardrobe: Tailored navy sheath dresses, pearl earrings, low heels.

name: Baek Jung-ho (“Mr. Baek”)
origin: Seoul; engineer at home; came to New York in 1971
occupation: Co-owner with his wife of Seoul Star Imports, a wig and handbag wholesaler on W 29th St
want: Buy the building his shop is in, so no landlord can price him out.
secret: He paid this year's surcharge with money from the merchants' rotating credit club his wife runs. If the shop fails, twelve families lose.

speech.pattern: Careful, formal English in short sentences; answers questions with questions; very dry humour.
samples: In Seoul I designed bridges. Here I sell wigs. Same mathematics.
You want twenty dollars for protection. From what? Please, show me.
My wife says trust nobody. My wife also says eat. I listen half.

haunts.why: Behind the counter, calculator in hand
Supper with other merchants
Watches delivery trucks; counts the envelopes

arc.act1: Refuses to pay a new 'fee' Teddy is sent to explain.
arc.act2: His purchase of Nick's building becomes Nick's lifeline, or Lisle's prize.
arc.act3: Brings the merchants to the march. Owns his building or loses it.

visual.silhouette: Slight and neat; very still when listening.
visual.wardrobe: White short-sleeve shirt, dark slacks, a cardigan even in July, black-framed glasses.
props: pocket electronic calculator (new and expensive in 1974, his pride)

name: Tina Mercado
origin: Mott Haven, the Bronx; Puerto Rican parents
occupation: Works the Eighth Ave strip; Delphine's closest friend; wants to do hair
want: Quit by Christmas and work the chair in Delphine's shop.
need: Stop covering for family who don't cover for her.
secret: Lonnie Gage is her cousin. Under threat, she's been passing him the club's meeting times, and the $1,100 Delphine lent her went to his lawyer.

speech.pattern: Fast and funny; Spanglish; nicknames for everyone; sings invented pop lyrics; deadly serious exactly once per scene.
samples: Del, that cop's so cheap he tips in subway tokens.
I'm gonna do hair. Hair don't hit you. Hair don't ask for a cut.
Rule twelve, Del: there is no rule twelve. I'm tired of rules.

haunts.why: Pie and complaints at 4 a.m.
Her corner, by the record shop
Presses her face to the glass with Delphine

schedule.note: Visits her mother in the Bronx

arc.act1: Comic relief with a bruise she won't explain.
arc.act2: The leak in the club is her, and Delphine starts to suspect it.
arc.act3: Confesses (M23). Either chooses Delphine over Lonnie in M27, or runs. She survives in every ending.

visual.silhouette: Small, quick and animated; high ponytail; big gold hoops.
visual.wardrobe: Bright pink wrap top, denim flares, platform sandals, a denim jacket at dawn.

name: Yiannis Doukas
origin: Kastoria, Greece; came in 1952 and learned the trade under Nick
occupation: Head cutter at Varelas & Co.; furriers' union shop steward
want: Keep his crew employed through a dead summer.
need: Decide whether loyalty to Nick is loyalty to the men.
secret: He counted the vault in June, knows it's short, and has said nothing out of loyalty.

speech.pattern: Blunt and accented; craft metaphors (skins, seams, nap); calls Nick 'Niko' when he's being honest.
samples: A skin tells you where it was cut. So does a man, Niko.
Thirty men in this loft. Summer, I have work for twelve. You tell me who.
Nobody counts a vault in June unless he's afraid of the number.

haunts.why: The cutting table under the north windows
Coffee, backgammon and union business

edges.note: Kallis wants him and the crew.

arc.act2: Knows exactly how many coats are in the vault during the brownout job, and makes Nick say it.
arc.act3: Takes the crew to the march, or to Kallis.

visual.silhouette: Wiry; forearms scarred from the knife; flat cap.
visual.wardrobe: White work smock dusted with fur, grey trousers, rubber-soled shoes.
props: furrier's knife (a work tool, never used as a weapon)
